hints: Focus on the three factors that control first ionisation energy: nuclear charge, atomic radius and shielding.
Compare the atoms: hydrogen is $1s^1$ with 1 proton, helium is $1s^2$ with 2 protons, and both electrons are in the same $n=1$ shell with no inner shells.
Ask yourself which change gives a much stronger pull on the $1s$ electrons and makes the electron far harder to remove.
walkthrough:
**Recall what controls ionisation energy**

Think of first ionisation energy as how strongly the nucleus holds the outer electron. It increases with higher nuclear charge, smaller distance, and less shielding.

$$\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^+\text{(g)} + e^-$$

**Compare hydrogen and helium side by side**

Hydrogen is $1s^1$ with a $1+$ nucleus. Helium is $1s^2$ with a $2+$ nucleus. Both use only the $n=1$ shell, so distance is very similar and there are no inner electrons to shield.

$$\text{H: 1 proton, 1 electron} \quad \text{vs} \quad \text{He: 2 protons, 2 electrons}$$

**Pick the causal factor**

The big difference is double the protons pulling on electrons in the same shell. That much higher effective nuclear charge pulls the $1s$ electrons in tighter, so much more energy is needed to remove one.

options.A: Pairing in the $1s$ orbital does not increase ionisation energy. Paired electrons actually repel each other slightly, which would make removal easier, not harder. This is the opposite effect to what is observed.
options.B: Saying the $n=1$ level is filled is just a description of helium's configuration. It does not explain why the electron is held more strongly. The stability of the full shell is a result of the high nuclear charge, not the cause.
options.C: Correct and causal. Helium has 2 protons compared to 1 in hydrogen, with both electrons in the same $n=1$ shell and almost no shielding. The doubled nuclear charge gives a much stronger attraction, so first ionisation energy is much higher.
options.D: There is no meaningful shielding difference here. Both H and He have only the $n=1$ shell and no inner shells of electrons to shield the nucleus. Shielding only becomes important from lithium onwards.
